title: Line up right, mirror the ones
allegory: Broadcasting is two dance troupes pairing up one to one: they line up from the right, a troupe with a lone dancer on a line stands before a mirror and is seen as many times as needed, and if both have several dancers but different counts the show stops.
map: formation cards lined up from the right
shapes compared from the last axis backwards
a missing line counts as one dancer
the shorter shape is left-padded with size-1 axes
a lone dancer seen many times in a mirror
a size-1 axis stretched as a stride-0 view, nothing copied
sizes differ and neither is 1: an error

cap.1: You add two lists of four numbers and get sixteen back. No error, no warning. Something quietly stretched them.
cap.2: x has shape (4,1) and y has shape (4,). x + y hands back a (4,4), not four numbers. PyTorch followed its rules exactly; the rules make this mistake legal.
cap.3: (4,1) + (4,) left-pads y to (1,4), then both expand to (4,4). The result is well-typed everywhere downstream, so the bug surfaces far from the line that caused it.

cap.1: Two troupes pair up one to one, lined up from the right. A lone dancer stands before a mirror and is seen as many times as the other troupe needs.
cap.2: Elementwise ops pair elements one to one. Shapes are compared from the last axis backwards; a missing axis counts as size 1, and any size-1 axis is repeated to match its partner.
cap.3: Align shapes at the trailing axis, left-pad the lower-rank operand with 1s, and expand each singleton axis to its partner's extent. The expansion is a stride-0 view: nothing is copied.

cap.1: Line the shapes up from the right. Wherever one side says 1, it gets mirrored to match the other. Here both troupes stretch, and you get a 3 by 4 by 5 block.
cap.2: (3,1,5) + (1,4,5) gives (3,4,5). Right to left: 5 matches 5, the 1 stretches to 4, and 3 stretches the other 1. Both operands expand, not just the smaller one.
cap.3: Per aligned axis the output extent is the larger size when the sizes are equal or one is 1; otherwise it raises. Each operand here has one singleton axis, so both expand into (3,4,5).

chapters.name: When it refuses
chapters.verdict: Shapes line up from the right, never from the left.

cap.1: The warm-up quiz asks which pairs break. The trap is lining shapes up from the left. Line them up from the right and 6 meets 2: the show stops.
cap.2: (8,2,6) + (8,2) looks like it should fit, but alignment starts at the last axis, so (2,6) sits against (8,2). Two clashes, so it raises. The [0.0] quiz is built from pairs like these.
cap.3: Left-padding turns (8,2) into (1,8,2), so the trailing comparisons are 6 vs 2, then 2 vs 8. Both fail. An intuition that aligns shapes from the left predicts success here and is wrong.

cap.1: The column of four meets the row of four. Mirrors fill the whole square: sixteen pairings. The four you actually wanted sit on the diagonal.
cap.2: y is left-padded to (1,4), then both stretch to (4,4): every x meets every y. You meant x[i] + y[i], which is only the lit diagonal. The other twelve are silent garbage.
cap.3: A mismatched MSE, preds (N,1) against targets (N,), averages all N² pairs: the loss falls far too slowly and memory grows with the square of the batch. Fix: assert preds.shape == targets.shape.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Backprop sums the mirrors back down
Every bias, batch and mask leans on it

cap.1: Broadcasting sits under almost every line of tensor maths you will write. Know the rules, check the shape you meant, and silent bugs stop being silent.
cap.2: Adding a bias to a batch, batching ray tracing, masking attention: all broadcasting. In backprop the stretched copies are summed back down (unbroadcast). Assert shapes at boundaries.
cap.3: When you read or edit activations to understand and steer a model, a silently broadcast (N,N) is a wrong answer that still looks like data. Shape asserts or jaxtyping at boundaries catch it.

coda.title: Shape A is (a, b) and shape B is (n,). How many numbers come out?

readouts.label: result
readouts.f: (b==n || b==1 || n==1) ? 'shape (' + a + ',' + max(b,n) + ')' : 'raises: ' + b + ' meets ' + n

caption.1: Start at A = 4 by 1 and B = 4 long: four and four go in, sixteen come out. Now set A's columns to 3 and watch it refuse.
caption.2: B is left-padded to (1, n), then every 1 stretches. a = 1, b = 4 gives the four matched sums you meant; a = 4, b = 1 gives sixteen; b = 3 against n = 4 raises.
caption.3: Each aligned axis takes the larger size when the sizes match or one is 1. The result can dwarf both inputs: 8 stored numbers in, 16 out, and nothing in the type system notices.

where_else: Adding a bias vector to every row of a batch
Unbroadcast in backprop: the gradient sums the stretched copies back down
Batched ray tracing in [0.1]: many rays tested in one expression
sum(dim=1) without keepdim=True, then dividing: the sums line up as a row, not a column

hamming.what: The rule that lets tensors of different shapes combine, by lining shapes up from the right and stretching size-1 axes.
hamming.when: Every elementwise operation between tensors whose shapes are not identical, which is most lines of tensor code.
hamming.why: It saves copies and loops, but it also makes the commonest shape mistake legal, so the habit that matters is asserting the shape you meant.

object.title: The mirror box
object.subtitle: A column and a row that a mirror turns into a square of sixteen.

knobs.label: Show only the pairs you meant

cap.1: One column of four towers: the troupe with a lone dancer on each line, shape (4,1). Nothing is stretched yet.
cap.2: x has shape (4,1): four rows, one column. Before broadcasting, it is just this.
cap.3: A (4,1) operand: extent 4 on axis 0, a singleton on axis 1 waiting to be expanded.

cap.1: The mirror stretches the column across four places, and the row of four rides on top. Sixteen towers from eight numbers.
cap.2: (4,1) + (4,) gives (4,4). Tower (i, j) is x[i] + y[j]: an outer sum, not four matched sums.
cap.3: Both singleton axes expand, then the add materialises a full (4,4): sixteen outputs from eight stored inputs.

cap.1: Look along any row: it climbs the same staircase as every other row. That staircase is y, mirrored down four rows.
cap.2: Every row repeats y and every column repeats x. The repeats are views of one stored copy, not new data.
cap.3: The broadcast axis has stride 0, so every index along it reads the same memory. Only the output of the add allocates.

cap.1: Keep only the diagonal: these four are the sums you meant. The other twelve are the bug.
cap.2: Matched pairs x[i] + y[i] are the diagonal. The silent broadcast computed the whole square.
cap.3: In an MSE with (N,1) against (N,), the mean runs over all N² entries instead of the N diagonal ones, so the gradient is averaged over wrong pairs.

predict.q: x is (4,1) and y is (4,). What does x + y give?

options.t: An error, because the shapes differ

predict.why: y is left-padded to (1,4), then both size-1 axes stretch. Legal, silent, sixteen numbers.

options.t: No: lined up from the right, 6 meets 2
Yes: the 8s and the 2s line up

predict.why: Shapes align at the last axis, so (8,2) sits under (2,6). Aligning from the left gets this wrong.

predict.q: When a size-1 axis is stretched, is the data copied?

options.t: No: it is a stride-0 view of the same memory
Yes: copies are tiled into new memory

predict.why: The stretch is a view. Only the result of the operation takes new memory.

object.where: Any outer sum or pairwise table: distance matrices, a bias added to every row, a mask laid over every attention score.
